examples.title: A service health dashboard from four objects
examples.body: Metric cards, a status table, a checklist and a latency chart composed into one grid. The same grid writes a PNG for chat and email and an HTML page for a browser.
examples.script:
# Service data from a monitoring API, a CSV export or Get-Counter.
$services = @'
Name,Status,Requests,P95
Gateway,Healthy,48210,84
Identity,Healthy,21980,112
Orders,Warning,15402,318
Search,Healthy,30117,146
'@ | ConvertFrom-Csv
$week = 182, 190, 201, 262, 310, 298, 214   # Orders p95, last seven days
$theme = 'Dark'

$total = ($services | Measure-Object Requests -Sum).Sum
$slowest = $services | Sort-Object { [int] $_.P95 } | Select-Object -Last 1
$healthy = @($services | Where-Object Status -eq 'Healthy').Count

# -PassThru returns the ChartForgeX chart, so the dashboard can embed it.
$latency = New-ImageChart {
    New-ImageChartLine -Name "$($slowest.Name) p95 (ms)" -Value $week
    New-ImageChartLine -Name 'Target' -Value (@(250) * $week.Count) -Color '#eeb640'
} -FilePath latency.png -Width 932 -Height 320 -Theme $theme -ShowGrid -PassThru `
    -Options (New-ImageChartOptions -ShowLegend -LegendPosition Bottom -TickCount 4)
# It is a ChartForgeX object, so its .NET API is one dot away.
[void] $latency.WithTitle("$($slowest.Name) latency").WithSubtitle('Last seven days')
[void] $latency.WithXLabels('Wed', 'Thu', 'Fri', 'Sat', 'Sun', 'Mon', 'Tue')

$table = New-ImageTableBlock -Title Services -Column Name, Status, Requests, P95 `
    -StatusColumn Status -Theme $theme -Row ($services | ForEach-Object {
        , @($_.Name, $_.Status, ([int] $_.Requests).ToString('N0'), "$($_.P95) ms")
    })
$checks = New-ImageListBlock -Title Checks -Theme $theme `
    -Item 'TLS expiry', 'Backups', 'Queue depth' -Value '41 days', 'OK', '1,204' `
    -Status Positive, Positive, Warning
[void] $table.WithSize(616, 270)
[void] $checks.WithSize(300, 270)

$card = @{ Width = 300; Height = 170; Theme = $theme }
$items = @(
    New-ImageMetricCard -Label Requests -Value $total -Format N0 -Status Positive `
        -Trend '+8% vs last week' -MiniValues 98, 101, 104, 110, 116 @card
    New-ImageMetricCard -Label 'Slowest p95' -Value ([int] $slowest.P95) -Unit ms `
        -Caption $slowest.Name -Status Warning -MiniValues $week @card
    New-ImageMetricCard -Label Healthy -Value "$healthy of $($services.Count)" `
        -Caption services -Status Positive @card
) | ForEach-Object { New-ImageVisualGridItem -Block $_ }
$items += New-ImageVisualGridItem -Block $table -ColumnSpan 2
$items += New-ImageVisualGridItem -Block $checks
$items += New-ImageVisualGridItem -Chart $latency -ColumnSpan 3

$grid = New-ImageVisualGrid -Title 'Service health' -Subtitle 'Week 41' -Columns 3 `
    -Gap 16 -Padding 24 -AdaptiveRowHeights -Theme $theme -Content $items
$grid | New-ImageVisualStory -FilePath service-health.png
$grid | New-ImageVisualStory -FilePath service-health.html

$services | Sort-Object { [int] $_.P95 } -Descending | Format-Table -AutoSize

----     ------  -------- ---
Orders   Warning 15402    318

Identity Healthy 21980    112
Gateway  Healthy 48210    84

examples.title: Trend against a target
examples.body: Two series, a target line and release markers. One definition renders PNG and SVG.
examples.script:
# Fourteen days of p95 latency, oldest first.
$p95 = 182, 175, 190, 188, 201, 240, 262, 310, 298, 214, 205, 198,
    190, 186
$target = 250

$series = @(
    New-ImageChartLine -Name 'Orders API' -Value $p95 -Smooth
    New-ImageChartLine -Name 'Target' -Color '#c78404' `
        -Value (@($target) * $p95.Count)
)
$events = {
    New-ImageChartAnnotation -X 6 -Y 0 -Text 'Release 4.2'
    New-ImageChartAnnotation -X 10 -Y 0 -Text 'Index fix'
}
$chart = @{
    Width    = 760
    Height   = 380
    XTitle   = 'Day'
    YTitle   = 'p95 latency (ms)'
    ShowGrid = $true
    Options  = New-ImageChartOptions -ShowLegend -TickCount 5
}

# One definition, two formats: the extension picks the renderer.
foreach ($file in 'latency-trend.png', 'latency-trend.svg') {
    New-ImageChart -Definition $series -FilePath $file @chart `
        -AnnotationsDefinition $events
}

$above = 1..$p95.Count | Where-Object { $p95[$_ - 1] -gt $target }
"Days above target: $($above -join ', ')"
"Peak: $(($p95 | Measure-Object -Maximum).Maximum) ms"

examples.title: Month-over-month cost bridge
examples.body: A waterfall from an ordered hashtable: the keys become labels, the values become steps.
examples.script:
# Last month's bill, then each change that moved it.
$steps = [ordered]@{
    September  = 4200
    Compute    = 380
    Reserved   = -250
    Storage    = 610
    Licences   = -140
}

New-ImageChart {
    New-ImageChartWaterfall -Name 'Cloud cost (EUR)' `
        -Value @($steps.Values) -Labels @($steps.Keys)
} -ShowGrid -FilePath cost-bridge.png -Width 640 -Height 340 `
    -Options (New-ImageChartOptions -ShowDataLabels -NoLegend)

$steps.GetEnumerator() | Format-Table -AutoSize `
    @{ Name = 'Step'; Expression = 'Key' },
    @{ Name = 'EUR'; Expression = 'Value' }
"October: {0:N0} EUR" -f ($steps.Values | Measure-Object -Sum).Sum

examples.title: The whole ChartForgeX API with -ChartScript
examples.body: When a cmdlet has no parameter for it, the script block receives the ChartForgeX chart: titles, category labels and stacked bars here.
examples.script:
$builds = @'
Day,Passed,Failed
Mon,41,3
Tue,38,6
Wed,45,2
Thu,52,4
Fri,47,1
'@ | ConvertFrom-Csv

# -ChartScript hands you the ChartForgeX chart itself, so every
# method in the .NET API is available, not only the cmdlets.
New-ImageChart -ChartScript {
    param($chart)
    # ChartForgeX loads in the module's own context: ask the chart
    # for its types instead of writing [ChartForgeX.Primitives...].
    $point = $chart.GetType().Assembly.GetType(
        'ChartForgeX.Primitives.ChartPoint')
    function ConvertTo-Point([double[]] $values) {
        $points = [Array]::CreateInstance($point, $values.Count)
        for ($i = 0; $i -lt $values.Count; $i++) {
            $points[$i] = $point::new($i + 1, $values[$i])
        }
        , $points
    }
    [void] $chart.WithTitle('Builds by result')
    [void] $chart.WithSubtitle('Week 41, main branch')
    [void] $chart.WithXLabels([string[]] $builds.Day)
    [void] $chart.AddBar('Passed', (ConvertTo-Point $builds.Passed))
    [void] $chart.AddBar('Failed', (ConvertTo-Point $builds.Failed))
    [void] $chart.WithStackedBars()
} -ShowGrid -FilePath chart-script.png -Width 640 -Height 360 `
    -Options (New-ImageChartOptions -ShowLegend `
        -LegendPosition Bottom -Palette '#11776f', '#d64545')

$builds | Format-Table -AutoSize

examples.title: Animated request flow
examples.body: A scenario walks a request across the map. SVG animates in the browser; GIF works in chat.
examples.script:
$nodes = @(
    New-ImageTopologyNode browser Browser -Kind Person -X 0 -Y 0
    New-ImageTopologyNode api 'Orders API' -Kind Service -X 260 -Y 0
    New-ImageTopologyNode db 'Orders DB' -Kind Database -X 520 `
        -Y 0 -Status Warning
)
$arrow = @{ Direction = 'Forward' }
$edges = @(
    New-ImageTopologyEdge browser api -Id call @arrow
    New-ImageTopologyEdge api db -Id query @arrow
)

# A scenario names the edges a request travels, in order.
$scenario = New-ImageTopologyScenario order 'Place an order' `
    -StepDefinition {
        New-ImageTopologyScenarioStep call Edge -Label 'POST order'
        New-ImageTopologyScenarioStep query Edge -Label 'Save order'
    }
$motion = New-ImageTopologyMotion -ScenarioId order `
    -DurationSeconds 3 -FramesPerSecond 10

$flow = @{
    Node = $nodes; Edge = $edges; Scenario = $scenario
    Motion = $motion; Layout = 'Manual'
    Width = 720; Height = 160; NoLegend = $true
    FitContentToViewport = $true
}
# SVG animates in the browser; .gif writes the same motion for chat.
New-ImageTopology @flow -FilePath request-flow.svg

$scenario.Steps | Format-Table Id, Kind, Label -AutoSize
examples.console:
Id    Kind Label
--    ---- -----
call  Edge POST order
query Edge Save order

examples.title: Animated terminal session
examples.body: Commands and output replayed as animated SVG, HTML or GIF for documentation and release notes.
examples.script:
# Rows from your own command. The story replays them; it never
# runs the commands it shows.
$health = @'
Name,Status,P95
Gateway,Running,84 ms
Orders,Degraded,318 ms
Search,Running,146 ms
'@ | ConvertFrom-Csv

$terminal = @{
    Title = 'pwsh'; WorkingDirectory = 'C:\Ops'; Theme = 'Dark'
    WindowStyle = 'WindowsTerminal'; Width = 640
}
$story = New-ImageConsoleStory @terminal -PassThru -Content {
    New-ImageConsoleStoryCommand 'Get-ServiceHealth -Env Prod'
    $health | New-ImageConsoleStoryTable -Property Name, Status, P95
    New-ImageConsoleStoryBlankLine
    New-ImageConsoleStoryCommand 'Restart-OrdersPool -WhatIf'
    New-ImageConsoleStoryOutput 'What if: restart 3 Orders nodes' `
        -Style Warning
    New-ImageConsoleStoryOutput 'Health check passed' -Style Success
}

# SVG and HTML replay in a browser; PNG keeps the final frame.
# .gif and .apng write the same animation for chat tools.
foreach ($ext in 'svg', 'html', 'png') {
    $story | Export-ImageConsoleStory -Path "console-story.$ext"
}

Get-Item console-story.* | Format-Table Name,
    @{ Name = 'KB'; Expression = { [int] ($_.Length / 1KB) } }
